finding.claim: The /invoice/<inv_id> route returns any invoice to any caller. It has no authentication and no ownership check (an IDOR / broken access control). The sibling /my/invoice/<inv_id> route does check ownership, so the missing check looks like an oversight.
finding.source: The inv_id URL path parameter, supplied by any HTTP client, including unauthenticated ones. No g.user is needed.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10, which returns the full invoice record (including the customer field and other billing data) for any customer.

trace.note: Route /invoice/<inv_id> is registered with no auth decorator.
INVOICES.get(inv_id) looks the record up by the attacker-supplied ID only; abort(404) fires only if the ID is missing.
The invoice is returned without comparing inv['customer'] to g.user['id']. Compare lines 16-17 in get_my_invoice, which do perform this check.

finding.guards_checked: This file is the whole codebase. It has no before_request hook, login_required decorator or other authentication middleware, and no role or ownership check on this route. g.user is never set anywhere in the file, so any authentication layer would have to live outside it. Even then, nothing here would stop one authenticated user from reading another customer's invoice. Invoice IDs may be guessable or sequential, which makes enumeration easier, but the missing check is exploitable whatever the ID format.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no decorator, before_request hook or ownership check and returns jsonify(inv) for any existing ID, unlike the check at invoices.py:16-17 in get_my_invoice; invoices.py is the only file in the directory.
